results.summary: This project implements a 3-bit one-hot decoder in Verilog. It takes three input bits and produces eight output bits, with exactly one output asserted for each valid input combination. The documentation is essentially a template with no explanation of how it works or how to test it. No external hardware or testing details are provided.

This project is a read-only memory that stores ASCII encodings of LaTeX code for typesetting Laplace transforms of common functions. It is controlled by an address input and a start signal, and it outputs the function and its transform character by character on two separate 8-bit output buses. The design uses two address spaces: one for the character data and one for pointers to each transform's start and length. It was verified on silicon and correctly recalled 43 Laplace transforms after a proper reset. The design requires an external clock and a way to provide the address and control signals.

This project implements a two-player Pong game in Verilog. It uses an 8x8 NeoPixel LED matrix as the display and six push buttons for control: two for each player's paddle movement, one to start the game, and one for reset. The game ends when the ball hits the left or right side of the matrix. External hardware includes the NeoPixel matrix and six push buttons with pull-up resistors.

This project is described as a 7-segment clock, but the documentation is a placeholder with no explanation of how it works or how to test it. The pin names suggest a serial data input and a data output with a valid signal, but the functionality is unclear. No external hardware or testing details are provided. The design is likely incomplete or undocumented.

This project is a module named reciprocal, but the documentation is a placeholder with no explanation of how it works or how to test it. The pin names indicate a single input and a single output, suggesting a combinational function. The author's tags mention inverse and piecewise-linear, but no further details are given. No external hardware or testing details are provided.

This project is a simple PWM generator with a variable duty cycle controlled by two buttons. It includes debounce logic for the buttons and uses a 4-bit counter to generate the PWM signal. The duty cycle can be increased or decreased by pressing the respective buttons. External hardware includes two push buttons with pull-down resistors and an oscilloscope to observe the PWM output.

This project is a 2-bit ALU with a 4-bit opcode that supports 16 operations including logical, arithmetic, shift, and comparison functions. It also includes a running sum mode that continuously adds the input to the output every second. The outputs are provided on an 8-bit bus and a 7-segment display interface. Testing can be done by connecting the outputs to LEDs or a BCD converter to observe the results. External hardware includes LEDs or a BCD converter for numerical output.

This project is a simple 8-bit ALU with six instructions selected by the three least significant bits of an instruction input. The operations include logical OR, NAND, NOR, AND, addition, and subtraction. The design is based on the Overture architecture from the game Turing Complete. Testing involves applying instructions and data inputs and verifying the 8-bit result output. No external hardware is required beyond input and output connections.

This project is a standalone test for a binarized Leaky Integrate and Fire (LIF) neuron, part of a larger experimental design from the Telluride Neuromorphic Workshop 2023. It supports eight binary inputs and binarized weights, accumulating them on an internal membrane that decays exponentially each clock cycle. When the membrane potential exceeds a threshold, the neuron emits a spike and the membrane is decreased. The only output is a binary spike signal. Testing involves holding reset to assign weights, then observing spikes after reset is released.

This project uses three rotary encoders to control three PWM generators, intended for mixing RGB LED colors. Each encoder is debounced and adjusts the duty cycle of its corresponding PWM output. The design provides three PWM outputs on the first three output pins. External hardware includes three digital rotary encoders and an RGB LED or other PWM-driven device. The documentation is brief but sufficient to understand the basic operation.
